candidateRows: God is the simplest and therefore most probable explanation of the universe and its most general features.
This states Swinburne's governing thesis and directly affirms the proposition under debate using his central probabilistic standard.
At the beginning of the proposition speech, Swinburne identifies simplicity and explanatory probability as the basis of his case for God.
Personal explanation through an agent's purposes, beliefs, and powers is a genuine explanatory mode alongside inanimate causal explanation.
The distinction supplies the explanatory category into which Swinburne places divine agency and is foundational to his overall inference.
Swinburne contrasts explanation by prior physical states and natural laws with explanation by an animate being's intentions, beliefs, and capacities.
Explanatory hypotheses are favored when they predict the evidence, avoid predicting contrary evidence, remain simple, and fit relevant background knowledge.
These criteria establish the inferential framework by which Swinburne later compares theism with rival explanations of the universe.
After distinguishing explanatory modes, Swinburne sets out the evidential, simplicity, and background-knowledge tests governing inductive explanation.
Simplicity favors hypotheses positing fewer entities, properties, and mathematical complications, as scientific theory choice illustrates.
Simplicity is the principal property Swinburne invokes to give theism a high prior probability over more complicated alternatives.
Using a robbery hypothesis and alternative gravitational laws, Swinburne argues that explanatory practice systematically prefers fewer and simpler postulates.
A perfectly good, omnipotent God has reason to create rational conscious beings capable of consequential choices between good and evil.
The move connects the proposed divine nature to the existence and morally significant capacities of human beings requiring explanation.
Swinburne derives goodness from unrestricted divine power and argues that freely choosing creatures are valuable rather than merely programmed agents.
Theism makes an orderly, life-producing universe with conscious beings probable, whereas such general features are very improbable without God.
This is the principal evidential comparison supporting the motion, applying simplicity and expectedness directly to the universe's general features.
Swinburne argues that embodied agency requires regular laws, that unguided uniformity and consciousness are unlikely, and that divine purposes predict both.
Swinburne's division between inanimate and personal explanation is incomplete because purposive explanation can apply to evolved or artificial inanimate systems.
The objection challenges the explanatory dichotomy that structures Swinburne's route from the limits of physical explanation to divine agency.
Swinburne's claim that explanation fundamentally divides into inanimate and personal forms.
Millican cites chess computers, evolved systems, animals, and plants to argue that purposive explanation need not entail a personal explanatory agent.
Simplicity is multifaceted and historically unreliable as a dominant scientific criterion, with descriptive and ontological simplicity capable of diverging.
The criticism attacks the key criterion Swinburne uses to assign theism a favorable prior probability over alternative explanatory hypotheses.
Swinburne's contention that theism's simplicity is the decisive basis of its prior probability.
Millican invokes scientific history and distinguishes concise specification, ontological economy, and computational complexity to undermine a unitary simplicity metric.
Discarding fit with background knowledge licenses magical divine explanations unlike observed causation, while scientific history has displaced intuitive purposive accounts.
The move challenges Swinburne's permission to exempt a cosmic explanation from coherence constraints and disputes the resulting appeal of purposive theism.
Swinburne's claim that a theory explaining the entire universe need not fit surrounding background knowledge.
Millican argues that bodiless instantaneous agency lacks experiential precedent and uses obsolete teleological theories and human bias to question its apparent simplicity.
A maximally simple creator hypothesis can be explanatorily hopeless because it is non-specific, whereas observed natural purposiveness depends on Darwinian and physical mechanisms.
The parody exposes a gap between verbal simplicity and explanatory informativeness, directly weakening the motion's inference from simplicity to probability.
Swinburne's claim that a simple omnipotent creator provides the most probable explanation of observed features.
Millican illustrates that an unrestricted creator can trivially explain any detail, then contrasts that vacuity with purposiveness explained through evolution and physical structure.
An infinite divine agent is not genuinely simple because its qualified powers and immense computational demands require substantial complexity.
It directly contests the simplicity criterion that supports the claim that God is the most probable explanation of the universe.
Swinburne's claim that an unlimited or infinite God constitutes the simplest personal explanatory hypothesis.
Millican argues that limitations concerning evil and free actions complicate the divine attributes, while the activity assigned to God implies extraordinary computational power.
A temporal God whose knowledge of future free actions is limited appears incompatible with the relativity of simultaneity.
It tests the internal coherence of the proposed divine attributes against a major physical theory used to describe space and time.
Swinburne's temporal account of God and his restriction on divine foreknowledge of the future actions of free agents.
Millican contends that a universal boundary between what God can and cannot yet know presupposes an absolute simultaneity that general relativity denies.
The freedom-based theodicy does not explain severe suffering that prevents victims from exercising morally significant agency.
The objection challenges whether the existence and distribution of profound suffering are probable under the proposed perfectly good creator.
Swinburne's claim that suffering is justified because it enables people to exercise morally significant freedom and responsibility.
Millican contrasts the proposed value of moral agency with infants and historical victims whose suffering or early deaths deprived them of meaningful opportunities to act.
Causal explanation ultimately divides into inanimate causation and purposive personal causation, while impersonal teleology fails as a stable alternative.
It defends the explanatory framework needed to present divine personal agency as a legitimate alternative to physical causal explanation.
Millican's contention that causal explanations need not be exhausted by Swinburne's categories of inanimate and personal explanation.
Swinburne rejects purposiveness without a purposive agent, interprets biological function through selection, and appeals to ordinary goal-directed action as clear personal causation.
Simplicity raises probability among hypotheses that fit the evidence, although a simpler hypothesis must be abandoned when it predicts the data less accurately.
The move supplies the methodological link between divine simplicity and probability that is fundamental to the proposition under debate.
Millican's argument that scientific practice sometimes accepts more complex theories and therefore does not uniformly favor simplicity.
Swinburne distinguishes simplicity from overall evidential success, uses scientific examples to explain their interaction, and argues that prediction requires an a priori simplicity preference.
Theism's generality produces too little precision to match the predictive success that can justify unfamiliar or complex scientific hypotheses.
It directly disputes whether the simplicity of theism translates into explanatory probability when the hypothesis lacks discriminating predictions.
Swinburne's appeal to scientific preferences for simple laws and to successful physics as support for accepting the divine hypothesis.
Millican accepts simplicity as a tiebreaker between equally successful laws but argues that scientific complexity earns support through precision whereas theism resists potential falsification.
Treating victims' suffering as a benefit because it enables other agents' morally serious choices is morally implausible.
It attacks the moral premise used to reconcile extensive grave suffering with the existence of an omnipotent and perfectly good creator.
Swinburne's claim that victims can benefit by providing opportunities for other people to make morally significant choices.
Millican argues that licensing starvation and slaughter for the moral seriousness of powerful agents cannot plausibly count as a good conferred upon their victims.
An independently created immaterial soul fits poorly with evolution, fine-tuning, and the development of the large human brain.
It challenges the coherence of combining divine fine-tuning and evolutionary history with a separately inserted locus of human thought.
Swinburne's view that human persons are immaterial souls contingently attached to evolved physical bodies.
Millican questions why a long evolutionary process and resource-intensive brains are necessary if God separately creates the immaterial component that performs human thinking.
God can ensure that sufferers receive lives worth living overall by providing compensating life after death.
The proposed compensation is a principal answer to cases in which earthly suffering otherwise appears incompatible with a good creator.
Millican's objection that some victims suffer or die too early for earthly freedom and moral development to justify their lives.
Swinburne argues that divine omnipotence enables posthumous compensation, that God is obligated to make each life good on balance, and that this follows from familiar theistic commitments.
Posthumous compensation neither follows from a terrible earthly life nor repairs the lost opportunity for victims to develop moral character.
It directly challenges the final compensatory mechanism offered to reconcile extreme earthly suffering with a perfectly good creator.
Swinburne's claim that God will compensate otherwise intolerable earthly suffering through a sufficiently good life after death.
Millican argues that bad earthly evidence gives no reason to expect later compensation and that prematurely killed children cannot posthumously recover the embodied character formation they missed.
